rationale: The entry's core (dew as the word descending from heaven) is directly established by Deut 32:2 and reinforced by the manna-dew mechanics (Num 11:9; Ex 16:14) plus the explicit manna-to-word equation (Deut 8:3). These texts, read together under the book's cross-reference method, carry the identification more tightly than the broader blessing reading. Secondary clauses (silent/nightly/morning appearance; word left as daily bread; rootless reception that evaporates under sun) follow immediately from the same passages plus the already-derived rain/seed/word pattern of the sower. The strongest counter (dew = divine blessing/favor) accounts for many other verses but does not unify the exact cluster printed with the entry as economically; blessing is the effect of the word, not a rival referent that displaces it. No material assertion printed in the entry itself is left unsupported by the cited evidence.
book_core_identification: Dew is the word of God descending from heaven.
book_secondary_elaborations: silent, nightly, found in the morning
manna falls upon the dew; when the dew lifts, the word lies on the ground as daily bread
received without root, it evaporates when the sun grows hot
chapter_only_objections: Pearl/moon/bride typology and calendar claims developed at length in the supporting chapter but never asserted inside the glossary entry
strongest_counter_interpretation: Dew primarily symbolizes divine blessing, favor, refreshment and life-giving provision (the silent moisture essential to fertility in an arid land), with the single simile of speech as dew remaining a secondary illustration rather than the governing referent.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the primary symbolic referent of dew is the word; the word reading is at best a local simile, while blessing/favor is the dominant and natural sense.
counter_case: Multiple independent blessing texts (Gen 27:28; Deut 33:13, 28; Hos 14:5; Ps 133:3; Zech 8:12) treat dew as the content of covenantal favor with no mention of teaching
Withholding of dew functions as judgment/drought (1 Kgs 17:1; Hag 1:10), again without reference to doctrine
Natural symbolism of life-giving moisture in the Near East makes blessing the expected default
Transience (Hos 6:4; 13:3) and resurrection (Isa 26:19) uses are acknowledged but remain secondary to blessing
book_explanatory_advantages: Unifies Deut 32:2 (speech distils as dew) with the manna-dew sequence and Deut 8:3's manna-equals-word equation into one continuous figure
Explains the precise physical mechanics (dew falls at night, lifts in morning, leaves the 'bread' behind) as the enacted parable of the word
Imports the already-established rain/seed/word pattern so that the sun-scorching of rootless reception is the same word under the same figure
Treats Hos 14:5 and Isa 26:19 as the life-giving effect of that word rather than unrelated senses
counter_explanatory_advantages: Covers a larger absolute number of dew occurrences that never mention speech or teaching
Aligns with the plain agricultural value of dew and with majority historical consensus
Handles pure blessing and judgment texts without additional interpretive steps
